Single acting and double acting shock absorbers differ primarily in how they generate damping force during vehicle operation:

- Single Acting Shock Absorbers [2]: These check only spring rebound, meaning they do not generate damping force during spring deflection. They are designed to provide damping only part of the time, requiring stiffer springs in the system and causing a slight preload on the suspension spring due to the return spring.

- Double Acting Shock Absorbers [2]: These provide damping during both spring compression and rebound. This allows for softer suspension springs and optimal damping in both directions. The damping force developed during spring compression is typically much lower than that developed during rebound, which is beneficial as it prevents transmitting shocks directly to the vehicle body upon impact.

These differences affect the overall performance of the shock absorber system, with double acting ones generally offering better ride quality and handling characteristics due to their ability to manage forces in both directions.

The relationship between indicated horsepower and brake horsepower involves mechanical efficiency. According to [4], "Mechanical efficiency within the engine is the relationship between the actual power produced in the engine (Indicated horsepower) and the actual power delivered at the crankshaft (brake or shaft horsepower). The actual power at the crankshaft is always less than the power produced within the engine due to frictional losses between many moving parts, and in four-stroke cycle engines, a great deal of horsepower is used to drive the valve train." Mechanical efficiency can be calculated by dividing brake horsepower by indicated horsepower [4].

- In contrast, in a three-quarter floating rear axle, the inner ends of the axle shafts can sometimes be secured with nuts, preventing their withdrawal without removing the differential cover. This means that the axle shafts are more rigidly connected to the wheels compared to the full-floating design [3].
